From this wording, I understand that there are use cases where having 128 bit hash output in digital signatures would be OK/allowed and some cases where it would be required to have 256 bits instead. Is that right?

However, the casual reader that I am is left wondering in which cases (in practice) it would be OK to only be (second) pre-image resistant.

Moreover the only secure hash algorithms which are allowed are 256 bits or more with the exception of SHA-1 which is only approved as part of HMAC-SHA-1. In practices, which algorithm with less than 256 bit output would I use to be conformant to this requirement? SHA-1? Truncated SHA-256?

One case that I am thinking of is OpenID connect `at_hash` and `c_hash` claims (of the ID token) which are defined as half of the hash of the access token and authorization code respectively using the hash algorithm associated with the ID token signature or MAC.

In practice, when using HS256, RS256 or ES256, the hash algorithm is SHA-256 so these claims would contain 128-bit truncations of SHA-256 hashes. Would that be allowed by this requirement?

**Question:** Do we need to make it clear that truncation of approved hash functions is OK? Is it always the case?

**Question:** I think, that in this example we are in the case where  (second) pre-image attack resistance is required? Because the access token and code are generated by the issuer?

If we take the two following snippets,

> Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures are collision resistant […] for collision resistance output lengths need to be at least 256 bits.

I'm concluding that hash functions used in digital signatures MUST have at least 256 bits output.

However at the same time we say:

> For (second) pre-image attacks, output lengths [of secure hash function used in digital signatures] of at least 128 bits

Is this sentence intended to apply to hash function used in digital signatures or to hash function in general?

> 6.6.4. Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures are collision resistant and have appropriate bit-lengths to avoid attacks, such as collision or (second) pre-image attacks.
>
> 6.6.5 Verify that when secure hash functions are used for security, their output lengths of at least 128 bits if second) pre-image resistance is required and 256 bit if collision resistance is required.

> If a particular implementation uses truncation in a cryptologically secure way this is also acceptable.

This part seems somewhat vague. (Does it actually allow using less than 256 bits? Should there be a minimum number of bits of security?)

For the first part, maybe something like this

> 6.6.4 [ADDED] Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures *schemes or as part of message authentication* are collision resistant and have a bit-length of at least 256 bits to avoid attacks, such as collision or pre-image attacks. If a particular implementation uses truncation in a cryptologically secure way this is also acceptable.

With this wording, this requirement would (deliberately) not apply to things such as:

* as [HOTP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4226.html), [TOTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6238) (which are heavily truncated HMAC);
* proof-of-work and such (?).
